prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the candidate on which this committee agrees most broadly: seven of eight members ranked it, five placed it in their top three and two placed it first. The case is a rare, clean chain of prediction and experiment. Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at a magic twist angle in 2011, and Jarillo-Herrero's group observed correlated insulating and superconducting states in 2018. That discovery opened moire quantum materials, in which interaction strength, band topology and filling are tuned with a gate in one clean platform. The work has been reproduced across many laboratories and extended to other moire systems and to fractional Chern insulators. The three credited names split naturally into theory and experiment and fit the three-laureate limit. I rank it above my own opening first choice for the reasons below.
statement.case_against: The field is only about eight years old and the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so a prize now risks being early. Experimental credit also extends beyond the single credited experimentalist: Yuan Cao as first author, and the parallel work of the Dean, Yacoby and Young groups, is not in the credit. Earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Santos and Peres is also outside it. I judge the discovery itself secure even if the microscopic explanation is not, but a colleague who weights maturity heavily can fairly resist.

responses.point: Ranked B046 eighth because the central observations date from 2018 and the origin of superconductivity and the correlated states is still being worked out.
responses.response: I take the maturity concern seriously and I do not dismiss it, since I also flagged slight prematurity in my opening. But the criterion is whether the discovery is secure, not whether every mechanism is settled. The phenomenology of correlated insulators and superconducting domes has been reproduced by independent groups across several moire platforms. The Mott-insulator, superconductor and Chern-insulator phases are measured facts, and their interpretation is a separate matter. Earlier prizes such as the 2016 topological-phase prize and the 2001 BEC prize were also given while the full theory was still developing. I would weight your reservation heavily only if reproducibility were in doubt, and it is not.

responses.point: Placed B046 first as a theoretical insight confirmed by a decisive measurement that created a widely imitated platform, while noting that Cao and other experimental groups are outside the credited set.
responses.response: I agree with the theory-plus-experiment framing and with the attribution caveat. I would add that the experimental allocation is the harder half. The supplied credit names one experimentalist where the 2018 papers had a team led by Jarillo-Herrero with Cao as first author. I still think the senior-investigator convention gives a defensible three-name prize, but we should say plainly that the discovery citation concerns the prediction and the observation and does not settle the experimental team's internal credit. I would not enlarge the set, because a fourth name is unavailable.

responses.point: Ranked cQED (B031) seventh and warned that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits may mean the area should wait. Also placed B041 first on a clean two-person atomic-physics case.
responses.response: I partly concede your timing point on circuit QED, and it is a main reason I moved B031 from first place to an alternative. The 2025 prize covered the foundation of superconducting circuits as quantum systems, and a prize for cQED so soon after would be a close follow-on, even though the discoveries are distinct. On B041 I agree that it is a strong, clean candidate. I disagree only that it should displace B046 this year, because its support is more concentrated (six members ranked it, but only three placed it in their top three). I keep it as my first alternative. I also see no reason to treat B041 and B046 as competing for the same slot in later years.

responses.point: Ranked circuit QED sixth, noting that Girvin's omission is unresolved credit and that the 2025 prize reduces the likelihood of near-term recognition of an adjacent topic.
responses.response: Your Girvin point is correct and I raised it myself. The 2004 theory proposal and the first strong-coupling demonstration had a larger author list than the credited trio, and Schoelkopf's group developed the transmon and readout after the first demonstration. I could not call that attribution clean, and combined with the timing issue it is a concrete reason why I no longer lead with B031 even though it is my own field. I do not agree that B018 is stronger on the ground of timing alone. You and I both placed it second, but Wineland's 2012 prize already honoured ion control and the experimental credit there is split.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the unsettled superconducting pairing mechanism as a barrier to recognition at about eight years.
How to handle experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero, in particular Yuan Cao and the parallel Dean, Yacoby and Young results, within a three-name limit.
Whether circuit QED (B031) should wait because of the 2025 prize or can be judged independently, and whether Girvin's omission can be resolved.
Whether B018 should be preferred over B046 given the overlap of the trapped-ion experimental credit with the 2012 prize.
statement.conflict_note: I rank circuit QED (B031) and I work in superconducting circuits, circuit and waveguide QED and quantum computing, and I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology at Chalmers, which hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize and where my colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work. For that reason I would consider recusing myself from any deliberation specifically on B031 and, to a lesser degree, from B018 and B010-type quantum-computing topics. My profile records no personal or collaborative link to any credited name on B046, so no specific conflict is apparent for my preferred configuration.
